Explain MVCC in databases.
Plan: retrieve the definition from knowledge_retrieval and paraphrase it.
MVCC keeps multiple versions of a row so readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers; commits are visible as of a transaction's start time.

MVCC — multiversion concurrency control — keeps several versions of each row, so readers work from a consistent snapshot while writers proceed without blocking them; each transaction sees data as of its start time.
What is an ETag and how is it used in caching?
Plan: pull the ETag semantics from knowledge_retrieval and summarise.
An ETag is an opaque validator per representation; clients send If-None-Match, the server replies 304 when unchanged, avoiding a body transfer.
An ETag is a validator string for a specific representation. Clients send it back in If-None-Match and the server answers 304 Not Modified when nothing changed, so the body is not transferred again.
Define cache coherence.
Plan: retrieve the definition and restate it precisely.
Cache coherence guarantees that all processors see a consistent view of memory: a write to an address becomes visible to every reader in a bounded order.
Cache coherence means every core sees a consistent view of memory — once one processor writes an address, that write becomes visible to all other processors in a bounded order.
What are generation counters used for?
Plan: look up generation counters in knowledge_retrieval.
A generation counter tags each read of shared state; if the counter advances before use, the reader knows its copy is stale and re-reads.
Generation counters stamp each read of shared state. If the counter moves on before the value is used, the reader knows its copy is stale and re-reads — a cheap staleness check without full locking.
What is the difference between semantic and syntactic caching?
Plan: retrieve both terms from knowledge_retrieval and contrast them.
Syntactic caches key on exact text; semantic caches key on meaning (embeddings), so paraphrased requests still hit.
Syntactic caching matches on exact strings, so only identical requests hit. Semantic caching matches on meaning via embeddings, so paraphrases of the same question are served from cache too.
What is a write-ahead log?
Plan: fetch the WAL definition from knowledge_retrieval.
A WAL records changes before they touch the main data files; after a crash the log replays committed changes, giving atomicity and durability.
A write-ahead log records every change before it is applied to the data files. On crash recovery the committed log entries are replayed, which is what gives the database atomicity and durability.
